title: Nearly 80% of Gen Z and Millennial Canadians say they don't feel financially secure: TD survey

body_markdown:
Half of Gen Z say up to $100,000 in the bank would be enough to feel secure, while 32% are motivated to invest more to improve their financial future.


TORONTO


, Nov. 17, 2026


/CNW/ -- What does it take to feel financially secure in Canada today? For Gen Z and Millennial Canadians, the answer is becoming increasingly complex. From managing rising everyday costs and pursuing homeownership to saving for the future and navigating major life milestones, many are balancing competing priorities at once. But a new TD survey suggests Canadians are defining financial security in ways that go beyond traditional financial milestones.


Key findings from this TD survey:


- 79% of Gen Z Canadians and 76% of Millennial Canadians say they don't feel financially secure, more than any other generation and Canadians overall (70%).
- 74% of Canadians, across every generation, believe that their generation has a harder time achieving financial security than previous generations.
- 80% of Canadians cite factors such as covering an unexpected expense or maintaining an emergency fund as most important to feeling financially secure.
- Gen Z is setting a lower threshold for financial security, with half (50%) saying they'd need up to $100,000 in savings and investments to feel financially secure, compared with 35% of Millennials and 32% of Canadians overall.


Canadians are redefining what financial security means to them


The survey findings suggest financial security isn't just about a dollar figure. Canadians are also looking at the steps they can take to help them feel more prepared for the future. When asked what contributes most to feeling financially secure, Canadians indicated:


- Staying prepared: Having safeguards in place such as being able to cover an unexpected expense or maintaining an emergency fund (80%).
- Planning ahead: Having a retirement savings plan, pension or long-term financial plan in place, including working with a financial advisor (62%).
- Making progress: Regularly contributing to savings and investment accounts, reaching personal goals, and maintaining investments over time (62%).


Investing appears to play a particularly important role for Millennials, with 42% saying regularly contributing to investments helps them feel financially secure, compared with 29% of Gen Z Canadians and 38% of Canadians overall.


"Financial security looks different for everyone and Canadians are measuring it by their ability to weather the unexpected, plan ahead and make progress toward their goals, not simply by the balance in their bank account," said Manish Jain, Vice President, Personal Saving & Investing, TD. "Building an emergency fund, having a financial plan and contributing regularly to savings and investments can all help strengthen your financial foundation. What's important is setting goals that work for your circumstances and taking consistent steps toward them."


Younger Canadians want to invest more and start earlier


For Canadians who feel financial security is becoming harder for their generation to achieve, that challenge may also be shaping how they think about building for the future. For Gen Z in particular, investing is emerging as one way they want to make progress:


- 27% of Canadians say they're motivated to invest more to improve their financial future, with Gen Z leading the way (32%).
- 21% of Canadians are motivated to start investing earlier, rising to 29% among Gen Z.


Gen Z is setting a different benchmark for financial security


While young Canadians are less likely to say they feel financially secure today, Gen Z may see financial security as achievable with less. Half of Gen Z Canadians say they'd need up to $100,000 in savings and investments to feel financially secure, compared with just 35% of Millennials and 32% of Canadians nationally.


"Financial security can sometimes feel like a moving target, but for many young Canadians it might be more achievable than it feels," said Leslie Logan, Senior Financial Planner, TD Wealth. "Start with a plan and begin contributing as soon as you can, with the amount that fits your lifestyle. And when you're not sure where to start or how all the pieces fit together, sitting down with a financial professional can help you talk through your goals and develop an approach that works for you. Investing consistently and staying invested over time can help you build strong habits, work toward financial security and benefit from the magic of compounding. As your circumstances change, you can revisit your goals and increase your contributions when it makes sense for you."


How Canadians can build greater financial security


How can Canadians make financial security feel more achievable?
Start with manageable goals that reflect your own finances. That can include making room in your budget for unexpected expenses by building an emergency fund and contributing regularly to longer-term savings and investments. Using TD client tools like[TD MySpend](https://edge.prnewswire.com/c/link/?t=0&l=en&o=4823821-1&h=741510751&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.td.com%2Fca%2Fen%2Fpersonal-banking%2Fsolutions%2Fways-to-bank%2Ftd-myspend&a=TD+MySpend) and checking in regularly on your finances can help you better understand your spending patterns. For Canadians balancing multiple priorities, working with a financial professional can also help them understand their options and develop a plan tailored to their circumstances and goals.


What can Canadians do when economic conditions are affecting their financial confidence?
While Canadians can't control the economy, they can focus on aspects of their finances they can influence. Setting aside emergency savings, reviewing spending and savings goals, and developing an investing approach that reflects their goals, time horizon and comfort with risk can help create a stronger financial foundation.


How much money do you need to start investing?


Investing doesn't necessarily require a large amount of money upfront. The amount of money you need to invest depends on your financial goals, what you can afford, and whether there are any minimum amounts that the investment product requires.


When investing in registered accounts at TD, such as a TD RRSP, you can contribute as little as $50 per month. However, some investment products may require a higher minimum amount.


For those interested in self-directed investing, options like partial shares and 100 free trades per year, available through[TD EasyTrade](https://edge.prnewswire.com/c/link/?t=0&l=en&o=4823821-1&h=3982914294&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.td.com%2Fca%2Fen%2Finvesting%2Fdirect-investing%2Faccounts&a=TD+EasyTrade) , can allow investors to start with smaller amounts, in some cases as little as $1.


Why can investing regularly make a difference?


Smaller amounts can add up over time, thanks to compounding interest. Setting up recurring investment amounts may also help you reach your financial goals faster, even during market downturns.


At TD, you can invest as little as $25 per transaction and adjust your contribution amount or frequency as often as you wish through[TD's Pre-Authorized Purchase Plan](https://edge.prnewswire.com/c/link/?t=0&l=en&o=4823821-1&h=3395840968&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.td.com%2Fca%2Fen%2Fpersonal-banking%2Fhow-to%2Feasy-web%2Fmutual-funds-set-up-a-preauthorized-purchase-plan&a=TD%27s+Pre-Authorized+Purchase+Plan) .


Building your knowledge, understanding risk, and investing consistently can help strengthen confidence and establish healthy long-term investing habits.


About the TD Survey


This TD survey was conducted using the Leger Opinion panel, which ran from October 26 – November 5th, 2026, with a nationally representative sample of 1,601 Canadian adults. The results were weighted by age, gender, and region (and in Quebec, language) to match the population, according to Census data. For comparison purposes, a probability sample of 1,601 has an estimated margin of error of ±2.4%, 19 times out of 20.
